items.readable_text:
Content:
Consider the curve [MATH: C] parametrized by the vector-valued function
[MATH: \mathbf f(t) = \langle t+1, \: t^2 +1\rangle, \qquad t \in (-\infty, \infty).]
Differentiating this function, we get
[MATH: \mathbf f'(t) = \langle 1, \: 2t\rangle.]

Content:
Evaluating this function and its derivative at [MATH: t=0,] we get the following pair of vectors:
[MATH: \mathbf f(0) = \left\langle 1, 1 \right\rangle, \qquad \mathbf f'(0) = \left\langle 1, 0 \right\rangle]

Content:
If we view [MATH: \mathbf{f}'(0)] as a vector attached to the tip of the position vector [MATH: \mathbf f(0),] then it will be tangent to the curve [MATH: C,] as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/f244365cdd2a183dc3615c66c8c160c3]

Content:
Since [MATH: \mathbf f'(0) \neq \mathbf{0},] it serves as a direction vector for the tangent line to the curve at [MATH: \mathbf f(0).] The equation of this line is given by

Content:
[MATH: R(u)|= f(0) + uf^{′}(0); = ⟨1, 1⟩ + u⟨1, 0⟩; = ⟨1 + u, 1⟩]

Content:
where [MATH: u \in (-\infty, \infty).]

Content:
In general, if a curve [MATH: C] is parametrized by a vector function [MATH: \mathbf f(t),] then the vector [MATH: \mathbf f'(t)] gives a tangent vector to [MATH: C] at [MATH: \mathbf{f} (t),] provided that [MATH: \mathbf f'(t)\neq \mathbf{0}.]

Content:
For a fixed [MATH: t] in the domain of [MATH: \mathbf{f}(t),] the equation of the corresponding tangent line is
[MATH: \mathbf{R}(u) = \mathbf{f}(t) + u\mathbf{f}'(t), \qquad u \in (-\infty, \infty).]

Content:
Furthermore, the vector [MATH: \mathbf f'(t)] always points in the direction that the curve [MATH: C] is oriented. In our example above, as [MATH: t] increases and passes through the point [MATH: (1,1),] the curve is transversed from left to right, and the direction of the vector [MATH: \mathbf{f}'(0)] is also from left to right.

items.title: Finding a Tangent Vector

sections.normalized_html: Find a tangent vector to the curve [MATH: \mathbf r(t)=t\,\mathbf i+t^2\,\mathbf j+t^3\,\mathbf k] at the point [MATH: P(1,1,1).]
sections.readable_text: Find a tangent vector to the curve [MATH: \mathbf r(t)=t\,\mathbf i+t^2\,\mathbf j+t^3\,\mathbf k] at the point [MATH: P(1,1,1).]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The point [MATH: P(1,1,1)] is at the tip of [MATH: \mathbf r(t)] for some specific value [MATH: t_0] of the parameter [MATH: t.] At this point, the vector [MATH: \mathbf r'(t_0)] is tangent to the curve.

First, we find the value of [MATH: t] that corresponds to [MATH: P.] We know that

[MATH: r(t)|= i + j + k; ti + t^{2}j + t^{3}k|= i + j + k,]

and equating the coefficients of [MATH: \mathbf i, \mathbf j,] and [MATH: \mathbf k] yields the following system:

[MATH: {t = 1; t^{2} = 1; t^{3} = 1] From the first equation, we get [MATH: t=1.] This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, [MATH: P(1,1,1)] is at the tip of the vector [MATH: \mathbf r(1).]

Now, we calculate [MATH: \mathbf r'(t)] and evaluate it at [MATH: t=1\mathbin{:}] [MATH: r^{′}(t)|= (d)/(dt)(t)i + (d)/(dt)(t^{2})j + (d)/(dt)(t^{3})k; = i + 2tj + 3t^{2}k; r^{′}(1)|= i + 2(1)j + 3(1)^{2}k; = i + 2j + 3k] Therefore, a tangent vector to the given curve at at the point [MATH: P(1,1,1)] is [MATH: \,\mathbf i+2\,\mathbf j+3\,\mathbf k.]

sections.readable_text: Find a parametrization of the tangent line to the curve [MATH: \mathbf r(t)=\left\langle \cos{t}, \: \sin{t},\: 4t^2\right\rangle] at the point where [MATH: t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Let [MATH: P] be the point at the tip of the vector [MATH: \mathbf r\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right ).] At this point, the vector [MATH: \mathbf r'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right )] is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at [MATH: P] can be parametrized as

[MATH: \mathbf R(u)=\mathbf r\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right )+u \, \mathbf r'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right ), \qquad u \in (-\infty, \infty).]

First, we find [MATH: \mathbf r\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \mathbin{:}] [MATH: r((π)/(2))|= ⟨\cos ((π)/(2)), \sin ((π)/(2)), 4((π)/(2))^{2}⟩ = ⟨0, 1, π^{2}⟩]

Now, we calculate [MATH: \mathbf r'(t)] and evaluate it at [MATH: t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\mathbin{:}] [MATH: r^{′}(t)|= ⟨(d)/(dt)(\cos t), (d)/(dt)(\sin t), (d)/(dt)(4t^{2})⟩; = ⟨ − \sin t, \cos t, 8t⟩; r^{′}((π)/(2))|= ⟨ − \sin ((π)/(2)), \cos ((π)/(2)), 8((π)/(2))⟩; = ⟨ − 1, 0, 4π⟩]

Therefore, the tangent line to the given curve at the point [MATH: P] where [MATH: t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}] is given by

[MATH: R(u) = ⟨0, 1, π^{2}⟩ + u⟨ − 1, 0, 4π⟩, u ∈ (− ∞, ∞).]

sections.normalized_html: Given the curve [MATH: \mathbf r(t)=\left\langle t^2+1\,,\, 6t+3\right\rangle,] find all of the points at which the tangent to the curve is perpendicular to the vector [MATH: \left\langle 3\,,\, 1\right\rangle.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, we calculate the derivative of [MATH: \mathbf r(t)\mathbin{:}] [MATH: r^{′}(t)|= ⟨(d)/(dt)(t^{2} + 1), (d)/(dt)(6t + 3)⟩; = ⟨2t, 6⟩]

The vectors [MATH: \left\langle 3\,,\, 1 \right\rangle] and [MATH: \mathbf r'(t)] are perpendicular for some value of the parameter [MATH: t] if and only if [MATH: \left\langle 3\,,\, 1 \right\rangle \cdot \mathbf r'(t) = 0.] So, we have

[MATH: ⟨3, 1⟩ ⋅ r^{′}(t)|= 0; ⟨3, 1⟩ ⋅ ⟨2t, 6⟩|= 0; 3 ⋅ 2t + 1 ⋅ 6|= 0; 6t + 6|= 0; t|= − 1.]

Therefore, the only solution is [MATH: t=-1.]

Finally, since

[MATH: r(− 1)|= ⟨(− 1)^{2} + 1, 6(− 1) + 3⟩ = ⟨2, − 3⟩,]

we conclude that [MATH: \left\langle 3\,,\, 1\right\rangle] and [MATH: \mathbf r'(t)] are perpendicular at the point [MATH: (2,-3).]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Consider the curve [MATH: C] parametrized by the vector-valued function
[MATH: \mathbf f(t) = \langle t+1, \: t^2 +1\rangle, \qquad t \in (-\infty, \infty).]
Differentiating this function, we get
[MATH: \mathbf f'(t) = \langle 1, \: 2t\rangle.]

Content:
Evaluating this function and its derivative at [MATH: t=0,] we get the following pair of vectors:
[MATH: \mathbf f(0) = \left\langle 1, 1 \right\rangle, \qquad \mathbf f'(0) = \left\langle 1, 0 \right\rangle]

Content:
If we view [MATH: \mathbf{f}'(0)] as a vector attached to the tip of the position vector [MATH: \mathbf f(0),] then it will be tangent to the curve [MATH: C,] as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/f244365cdd2a183dc3615c66c8c160c3]

Content:
Since [MATH: \mathbf f'(0) \neq \mathbf{0},] it serves as a direction vector for the tangent line to the curve at [MATH: \mathbf f(0).] The equation of this line is given by

Content:
[MATH: R(u)|= f(0) + uf^{′}(0); = ⟨1, 1⟩ + u⟨1, 0⟩; = ⟨1 + u, 1⟩]

Content:
where [MATH: u \in (-\infty, \infty).]

Content:
In general, if a curve [MATH: C] is parametrized by a vector function [MATH: \mathbf f(t),] then the vector [MATH: \mathbf f'(t)] gives a tangent vector to [MATH: C] at [MATH: \mathbf{f} (t),] provided that [MATH: \mathbf f'(t)\neq \mathbf{0}.]

Content:
For a fixed [MATH: t] in the domain of [MATH: \mathbf{f}(t),] the equation of the corresponding tangent line is
[MATH: \mathbf{R}(u) = \mathbf{f}(t) + u\mathbf{f}'(t), \qquad u \in (-\infty, \infty).]

Content:
Furthermore, the vector [MATH: \mathbf f'(t)] always points in the direction that the curve [MATH: C] is oriented. In our example above, as [MATH: t] increases and passes through the point [MATH: (1,1),] the curve is transversed from left to right, and the direction of the vector [MATH: \mathbf{f}'(0)] is also from left to right.

---

Item 2 — Example: Finding a Tangent Vector

Example Prompt:
Find a tangent vector to the curve [MATH: \mathbf r(t)=t\,\mathbf i+t^2\,\mathbf j+t^3\,\mathbf k] at the point [MATH: P(1,1,1).]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The point [MATH: P(1,1,1)] is at the tip of [MATH: \mathbf r(t)] for some specific value [MATH: t_0] of the parameter [MATH: t.] At this point, the vector [MATH: \mathbf r'(t_0)] is tangent to the curve.

First, we find the value of [MATH: t] that corresponds to [MATH: P.] We know that

[MATH: r(t)|= i + j + k; ti + t^{2}j + t^{3}k|= i + j + k,]

and equating the coefficients of [MATH: \mathbf i, \mathbf j,] and [MATH: \mathbf k] yields the following system:

[MATH: {t = 1; t^{2} = 1; t^{3} = 1]
From the first equation, we get [MATH: t=1.] This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, [MATH: P(1,1,1)] is at the tip of the vector [MATH: \mathbf r(1).]

Now, we calculate [MATH: \mathbf r'(t)] and evaluate it at [MATH: t=1\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: r^{′}(t)|= (d)/(dt)(t)i + (d)/(dt)(t^{2})j + (d)/(dt)(t^{3})k; = i + 2tj + 3t^{2}k; r^{′}(1)|= i + 2(1)j + 3(1)^{2}k; = i + 2j + 3k]
Therefore, a tangent vector to the given curve at at the point [MATH: P(1,1,1)] is [MATH: \,\mathbf i+2\,\mathbf j+3\,\mathbf k.]

[IMG: /graphics/1d982638f3bd912bc8329318369e03d5]

Item 5 — Example: Finding a Tangent Line to a Curve

Example Prompt:
Find a parametrization of the tangent line to the curve [MATH: \mathbf r(t)=\left\langle \cos{t}, \: \sin{t},\: 4t^2\right\rangle] at the point where [MATH: t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let [MATH: P] be the point at the tip of the vector [MATH: \mathbf r\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right ).] At this point, the vector [MATH: \mathbf r'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right )] is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at [MATH: P] can be parametrized as

[MATH: \mathbf R(u)=\mathbf r\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right )+u \, \mathbf r'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right ), \qquad u \in (-\infty, \infty).]

First, we find [MATH: \mathbf r\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \mathbin{:}]
[MATH: r((π)/(2))|= ⟨\cos ((π)/(2)), \sin ((π)/(2)), 4((π)/(2))^{2}⟩ = ⟨0, 1, π^{2}⟩]

Now, we calculate [MATH: \mathbf r'(t)] and evaluate it at [MATH: t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: r^{′}(t)|= ⟨(d)/(dt)(\cos t), (d)/(dt)(\sin t), (d)/(dt)(4t^{2})⟩; = ⟨ − \sin t, \cos t, 8t⟩; r^{′}((π)/(2))|= ⟨ − \sin ((π)/(2)), \cos ((π)/(2)), 8((π)/(2))⟩; = ⟨ − 1, 0, 4π⟩]

Therefore, the tangent line to the given curve at the point [MATH: P] where [MATH: t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}] is given by

[MATH: R(u) = ⟨0, 1, π^{2}⟩ + u⟨ − 1, 0, 4π⟩, u ∈ (− ∞, ∞).]

Item 8 — Example: Finding Points Where a Tangent Vector is Perpendicular to Another Vector

Given the curve [MATH: \mathbf r(t)=\left\langle t^2+1\,,\, 6t+3\right\rangle,] find all of the points at which the tangent to the curve is perpendicular to the vector [MATH: \left\langle 3\,,\, 1\right\rangle.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we calculate the derivative of [MATH: \mathbf r(t)\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: r^{′}(t)|= ⟨(d)/(dt)(t^{2} + 1), (d)/(dt)(6t + 3)⟩; = ⟨2t, 6⟩]

The vectors [MATH: \left\langle 3\,,\, 1 \right\rangle] and [MATH: \mathbf r'(t)] are perpendicular for some value of the parameter [MATH: t] if and only if [MATH: \left\langle 3\,,\, 1 \right\rangle \cdot \mathbf r'(t) = 0.] So, we have

[MATH: ⟨3, 1⟩ ⋅ r^{′}(t)|= 0; ⟨3, 1⟩ ⋅ ⟨2t, 6⟩|= 0; 3 ⋅ 2t + 1 ⋅ 6|= 0; 6t + 6|= 0; t|= − 1.]

Therefore, the only solution is [MATH: t=-1.]

Finally, since

[MATH: r(− 1)|= ⟨(− 1)^{2} + 1, 6(− 1) + 3⟩ = ⟨2, − 3⟩,]

we conclude that [MATH: \left\langle 3\,,\, 1\right\rangle] and [MATH: \mathbf r'(t)] are perpendicular at the point [MATH: (2,-3).]
